item.content:encoded:
The World Series is about to begin, and we’re being treated to a doozy of a series between the Brewers and the Rays. However, for the 28 other teams, they are turning their attention to 2027, so we’ll join them in that for a bit with some starting pitcher rankings for next season.
This is now my fourth year publishing my starting pitcher rankings and my second year doing it this early. In many ways, I like doing a first pass at rankings this year. At this point, it’s hard to overthink. Most players aren’t playing games or posting videos of new pitches, so there is nothing to get geeked about. Instead, these rankings are more “gut feel” rankings based on how I feel about all of these pitchers at the end of the season. While I tried not to get too in the weeds about stats, I did look back at the general profile that allowed a pitcher to finish among the top 30 overall starters in recent years, and tried to prioritize pitchers who fit that profile, which mostly meant elevating pitchers who get swings and misses, and penalizing pitchers who don’t seem like a good bet for a full season of innings.
As always, the pitchers are split into tiers based on their skillset or what they’ll provide your fantasy team. The tiers themselves are more important than the rankings inside the tiers, so I wouldn’t split hairs over a few spots in the rankings. I’ve also ranked these pitchers as if I’m doing a 12-team league, so safe but boring low-end starters take a hit in value, etc. I won’t have really long write-ups here, but I’ll be back with updated rankings after the new year, where we can get a little more into the nitty-gritty of the rankings.
OK? Ok, so let’s get started.
2027 Fantasy Baseball Starting Pitcher Rankings
| Rank | Player | Team | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| Aces | | | | |
| 1 | Jacob Misiorowski | MIL | No | Aces |
| 2 | Tarik Skubal | Free Agent | No | Aces |
| 3 | Cam Schlittler | NYY | No | Aces |
| 4 | Cristopher Sánchez | PHI | No | Aces |
| 5 | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | LAD | No | Aces |
There’s not much to discuss about these aces. All five posted a K-BB% of at least 21%, and four of them carried a Stuff+ of 113 or higher. They seem like the clear top five starters in baseball, if they can remain healthy.
| Fringe Young Aces | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 6 | Chase Burns | CIN | No | Young power arms |
| 7 | Payton Tolle | BOS | No | Young power arms |
| 8 | Logan Gilbert | SEA | No | Strikeout guys |
| 9 | Paul Skenes | PIT | No - Maybe? | Young power arms |
There’s an argument to be made for all of these guys being aces. Obviously, Paul Skenes is the key name because he was an ace coming into last season and then posted a
3.82 ERA with a 3.34 SIERA. His Stuff+ also fell from 110 in 2025 to 99 this past season, and he didn’t look fully healthy. Still, he’s one year removed from a 1.97 ERA over 187 IP and was the best young arm in baseball. It’s hard to completely ignore 2024 and 2025. All four of these guys finished with a K-BB% between 20% and 22%, and all are power-first pitchers. Chase Burns threw 154.1 IP with a 2.86 ERA, 3.46 SIERA, 14.4% SwStr%, and 112 Stuff+, and I think that innings number will rise, which will give him even more value. Payton Tolle’s first full season was 148.2 IP with a 3.03 ERA, 21.7% K-BB, and 115 Stuff+. Like Burns, I also expect his innings to rise and his value to tick up.
| Aces With Injury Risk | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 10 | Chris Sale | ATL | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 11 | Garrett Crochet | BOS | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 12 | Jacob deGrom | TEX | No (Previous risk) | Elite vets, health risk |
| 13 | Zack Wheeler | PHI | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
| 14 | Bryan Woo | SEA | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 15 | Jesús Luzardo | PHI | No | Elite vets, health risk |
| 16 | Dylan Cease | TOR | Yes | Elite vets, health risk |
If you wanted to take any of these starters over the guys in the tier above, that wouldn’t be crazy. They’re not down in this tier because they’re worse pitchers; they’re in this tier because they carry more injury risk than the pitchers in the tier above, and injury risk with your ace is a serious gamble. Chris Sale and Jacob deGrom have been healthy the last two years, but have a lengthy injury history, while Garrett Crochet missed essentially the entire year with an injury, and Dylan Cease saw his velocity plummet at the end of the season and then ended the year on the IL with a shoulder injury. You draft this group for ace outcomes at a price that already reflects the innings risk.
| Ace Upside - Limited Track Record | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 17 | Drew Rasmussen | TBR | No (Previous Risk) | WHIP guys |
| 18 | Cade Cavalli | WSN | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 19 | Braxton Ashcraft | PIT | No | Rising arms, unproven |
| 20 | Logan Henderson | MIL | Coming off injury | Rising arms, unproven |
| 21 | Gavin Williams | CLE | No | Rising arms, unproven |
Almost everyone here has one strong season to point to, which is why the tier name fits. Of course, Drew Rasmussen has more than one good season, but he also has had three elbow surgeries and has only pitched over 150 innings once in his MLB career. That prevents me from drafting him where I think his talent should have him because he carries so much extra risk. Cade Cavalli and Logan Henderson also have injury track records that make me a little bit concerned about their durability, and Cavalli’s breakout 2026 season was so closely tied to a velocity increase that I’m just not sure if I want to fully ignore the first three months of the season for him, which were pretty inconsistent. This feels like a fair hedge on the bets for Cavalli. Gavin Williams arguably has the best skills of the group (2.95 SIERA, 25.1% K-BB, 15% SwStr%), but he also had a 3.76 ERA because he is prone to losing his command for an inning in basically every outing.
| High-End SP2 Without Elite K% | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 22 | Parker Messick | CLE | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 23 | Max Fried | NYY | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
| 24 | Griffin Jax | TBR | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 25 | Hunter Brown | HOU | Yes | Weak contact and durability |
These four are valuable because of ERA and WHIP, not big strikeout totals. Parker Messick had moments where he looked like a fantasy ace, but he has just a 97 Stuff+ and his strikeout rate is not the same as the guys in the tier above. Max Fried had another solid season, but his fantasy finishes over the last four years have been super inconsistent because he seems to always miss time with an injury. Hunter Brown was clearly hurt and not pitching well this season, but his strikeout numbers also fell off a cliff in the second half of last season, so I’m not sure we can really rely on him for strikeouts. Griffin Jax is an interesting bet because he only moved into the rotation in the middle of the season, but he had 103.1 innings as a starter and registered a 3.14 ERA, 18.8% K-BB, and 13.6% SwStr%. That’s pretty damn good.
| There’s an Ace in There Somewhere | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 26 | Joe Ryan | MIN | Yes | Strikeout guys |
| 27 | Jared Jones | PIT | Yes | Rising arms, unproven |
| 28 | Reid Detmers | LAA | No | Rising arms, unproven |

| 32 | Nolan McLean | NYM | No | Young power arms |
| 33 | Eury Pérez | MIA | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 34 | Emmet Sheehan | LAD | No | Rising arms, unproven |
This tier is a bet on ceiling, and the group has the skills to justify it, but not the track record of consistent production. Obviously, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani, and Carlos Rodon are all in here because of injury concerns that prevent me from giving them enough innings to have them qualify as an ace. Reid Detmers finally had his breakout year in 185.0 innings with a 3.36 ERA and 22.0% K-BB, and Jared Jones shook the rust after his return from injury and pitched 101.2 innings with a 3.28 SIERA and 22.2% K-BB. He really came on at the end of the season. We also still see enough strikeout upside and raw, natural ability from Nolan McLean, Eury Perez, and Emmet Sheehan to have them here. I do worry that McLean had just a 9.6% swinging strike rate, and there may not be as much strikeout upside as people want to believe. This is the range that Misiorowski and Schlittler were going last year, and somebody in here is going to make that jump.
| No Longer Aces, But Safe Floor | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 35 | Gerrit Cole | NYY | No | Strikeout guys |
| 36 | Sonny Gray | BOS | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 37 | Shota Imanaga | Free Agent | No | WHIP guys |
| 38 | Logan Webb | SFG | No | Contact managers, low strikeout |
| 39 | Freddy Peralta | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 40 | Sandy Alcantara | MIA | No | Weak contact and durability |
The pitchers here have a long record of quality, and the case for them is volume and ratios. Sandy Alcantara is probably the weakest of the bunch, but he threw 211 innings this season, and we’re back to getting that bulk production from him; a 4.24 SIERA is just not ideal. Freddy Peralta has turned his season around with the Rays, and we’ve seen him be a good starting pitcher for too long to not assume he can continue to pitch well in 2027.
| Fun Upside With Volatility | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 41 | Ian Seymour | TBR | No | Strikeout guys |
| 42 | Andrew Painter | PHI | No | Strikeout guys |
| 43 | Christian Scott | NYM | No | Power arms, command concern |
| 44 | Kade Anderson | SEA | No | Top prospects, clear 2027 job |
| 45 | Kaima Taira | Intl (NPB) | No | International, unproven |
| 46 | Walbert Ureña | LAA | No | Low-strikeout, command concern |
The appeal here is strikeout ability, and the risk is large, which is why they’re all down in this range. Ian Seymour flashed the best MLB skills in the tier. In 77 innings as a starter this season, he posted a 2.84 SIERA, 26.7% K-BB, and 14.4% SwStr%. I know the 4.44 ERA wasn’t tremendous, but I believe in the underlying skill set here. Andrew Painter made some key pitch mix changes in the second half of the season that I really like, but, much like Cavalli, his ability to hold velocity will be crucial. Walbert Ureña is confusing. He throws hard and has a nasty changeup plus a sweeper that flashed the ability to miss bats this season. You watch him pitch, and you see a potential stud. But his four-seamer is pretty average, and his 4.14 SIERA and 12.3% K-BB% say he got lucky this season.
The two biggest wild cards here are Kade Anderson and Kaima Taira. Anderson was the top pitching prospect in baseball, but he relies on command and movement over velocity and raw stuff, so it remains to be seen how that translates at the big league level. Taira is almost certain to come over from Japan this offseason after pitching to a 1.36 ERA and 0.97 WHIP with 134 K and 44 BB over 139 IP in NPB this year. We’ve heard he touches 100 mph, has an eight-pitch mix, and could be the best pitching free agent this offseason, other than Skubal.
| Boring But It Can Work | | | Injured Season? | Pocket/Grouping |
| 47 | Kevin Gausman | Free Agent | No | Weak contact and durability |
| 48 | Aaron Nola | PHI | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
| 49 | George Kirby | SEA | No | Command-first, strikeout upside |
All of these guys had pretty gross ERAs but underlying metrics that say they pitched better than the results. We just have to decide if we believe that or not. Aaron Nola made some pitch mix changes in the second half (limiting elevated fastballs) that helped him to produce better results, but George Kirby simply never got it going this year. The draft case for each of these guys is innings, a discounted price based on ERA over SIERA, and a decent chance of a bounce-back, with Kevin Gausman the safest of the three, depending on where he signs.

This is another tier of injuries. These guys ended the season hurt or were hurt for basically the entire year. However, all of them seem likely to begin the year healthy and on the mound for their respective teams. You’re drafting them if the injury discount leaves a bigger gap than the missed time justifies.

These pitchers have flashed the physical tools, but the consistent results are not there yet. Roki Sasaki, Taj Bradley, and Sean Burke all had stretches in 2026 where they showed clear improvement from 2025. But those stretches didn’t last. Can we count of them in 2027? Trey Yesavage and Jackson Jobe both spent most of the year recovering from injury, but they are top pitching prospects who have shown upside when on the mound. Didier Fuentes was lights out in relief for Atlanta and should get a chance to start, and River Ryan figures to be in the rotation for the Tigers after being the headliner in the Skubal deal. He has flashed real ability before, but he needs to stay healthy.

These pitchers win with walks and contact, not strikeouts, and many have a Stuff+ under 100 (Tyler Mahle 88, Jake Bennett 93, Ranger Suarez 94, Michael King 95). Some of these guys have been top 30 pitchers before and potentially could again, but the ceiling just doesn’t feel overly high. I would draft this group for innings and WHIP, especially in deeper formats.

Every pitcher here has had a good stretch, but none has strung together a full good year. Some of that is due to injury (Bryce Miller and Connelly Early), but there is just a lot of volatility in this group. Even pitchers that have had good full seasons, like Andrew Abbott, have seemingly never had the profile to back up that success. I do like guys like Early, Miller, Joey Cantillo, or MacKenzie Gore as late-round flyers just in case they can ever put it together or stay healthy.

item.content:encoded:
When the 2026 Major League Baseball season officially comes to an end, the next big thing to watch is going to be what happens with two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal.
Skubal is the biggest free agent prize of the year, without a doubt. He follows in the footsteps of guys like Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto and Kyle Tucker, who were the biggest free agents of the year over the last three years. This year, it's time for Skubal to cash in.
Beyond Skubal, the biggest free agents of the offseason are Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Robbie Ray, Shota Imanaga and potentially Bo Bichette. Bichette has an opt-out in his deal with the New York Mets. It's going to be a fun few months across the league. Let's try our hand at projecting what it could cost to sign these top names.
Tarik Skubal — Starting Pitcher
Skubal's stint in free agency is going to be fascinating. On one hand, you have the hurler who has been the most dominant starter in baseball over the last three years, at least. On the other hand, Skubal is heading to free agency at 29 years old and after undergoing elbow surgery earlier in the season.
Skubal is the best player heading to the open market and he will get paid well. He even could get paid historically well. ESPN's Jeff Passan shared in a column that if there is no salary cap, he could double the $245 million deal Stephen Strasburg got from the Washington Nationals, at most. Arguably, that is far too high. Yoshinobu Yamamoto has the largest contract for a starter in big league history at $325 million over 12 years, but he got that at 25 years old. Gerrit Cole is a closer equivalent. He got his nine-year, $324 million deal at 29 years old. Skubal should come in much closer to that from a years perspective. But could very well top Yamamoto's overall value.
Projection: 8-years, $335 million ($41.8 AAV).
Randy Arozarena — Outfielder
Arozarena is a three-time All-Star, including each of the last two years, and is coming off a 5.7 WAR season. He picked a good time to have one of the best seasons of his career. Arozarena is the best non-Bichette bat heading to the open market, which should do wonders for his value.
Projection: 5-years, $120 million
Seiya Suzuki — Outfielder
Suzuki is the second-best non-Bichette offensive player heading to the open market. He's coming off a season in which he hit 26 home runs, drove in 86 runs and logged 31 doubles in 143 games played. He'll be 32 years old when the 2027 season begins. He should do quite well this winter.
Projection: 4-years, $90 million
Robbie Ray — Starting Pitcher
Ray may be 35 years old, but he can still get it down. He had a 3.59 ERA in 31 total appearances in 2026, including 30 starts, with the San Francisco Giants and the San Diego Padres. He was an All-Star in 2025. Ray won't turn 36 years old until October, 2027. He should get one more multi-year deal this offseason.
Projection: 3-years, $55 million
Shota Imanaga — Starting Pitcher
Imanaga is just 33 years old and hasn't had more than a 3.77 season ERA in his three-year big league career. He's younger than Ray and has been arguably better over the last three seasons. He should do even better in free agency.
Projection: 3-years, $64 million
Bo Bichette — Infielder
Bichette is going to be among the most intriguing players to follow over the next few weeks. Skubal is clearly the best free agent heading to the open market. If Bichette opts out, he'll be the second-best. Bichette is owed $42 million from the Mets, if he sticks around in 2027. Then, he has a $42 million player option for 2028.
It's hard to believe, but Bichette is still just 28 years old. If he were to enter the open market again, there should be a massive deal with his name on it.
Projection: 6-Years, $200 million

item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)

item.content:encoded:
It didn't take long for free agent rumors to start swirling.
The Chicago Cubs were just swept by the San Diego Padres in the National League Wild Card Round a few days ago, and free-agent rumors are already circling the baseball world.
It will no doubt be a busy offseason for the Cubs, who have plenty of players hitting free agency. Players like Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, David Peterson, and Carson Kelly will all test the open market this winter.
However, the biggest question mark this offseason for the Cubs is what they plan to do with their outfield. Both Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki are free agents at the conclusion of this year's World Series. That leaves the team in a potential rough spot.
The Cubs have to answer one of these questions ahead of free agency:
- Do we bring back both Happ and Suzuki and simply run it back with the same outfield core?
- Do we pay Happ and let Suzuki walk, since he will cost much less?
- Do we pay Suzuki big money and let Happ walk because Suzuki gives us the best chance to win?
The front office will obviously weigh all these options ahead of free agency. However, it seems as if the Cubs have already made somewhat of a decision about Suzuki's future with the organization.
Patrick Mooney of The Athletic reported that "it's unlikely that the Cubs will get into a bidding war for Suzuki's services, let alone win one."
Hearing that the Cubs won't enter a bidding war for Suzuki doesn't bode well for their chances of getting him back. Teams like the Dodgers, Blue Jays, and Yankees are better suited to get into a bidding war for the slugger than the North Siders.
Mitch Bannon of the Athletic already reported that the Blue Jays will pursue Suzuki this offseason. Given that Toronto isn't afraid to spend on big-time players (e.g., Dylan Cease last offseason), there's a strong chance that the outfielder doesn't re-sign with the Cubs.
Losing Suzuki in free agency would be a big loss for the North Siders. He has been one of the team's best power hitters since the Cubs signed him out of Japan in 2022. The Japanese slugger has 113 home runs over his five MLB seasons and has 58 home runs with 189 RBI combined over the past two years.
The Cubs would be losing that power bat at the top of their lineup if he goes to another team. Unfortunately, it's very possible he does leave.

item.content:encoded:
SAN DIEGO — Was it a successful season in Wrigleyville?
It’s hard — even with baseball’s highest scoring lineup, best defense and best player — to judge 2026 as anything but a failure for the Cubs.
They set championship-level expectations and World Series goals.
Bowing out of the postseason after two games, their offense muzzled and MVP center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong a non-factor, before the calendar even flipped to October?
They didn’t come close.
“The goal is to win, and we didn’t play well enough to do that,” third baseman Alex Bregman said. “It’s time to look in the mirror and get better.
“I know myself and a lot of these guys will be thinking about it every day of the offseason and let it fuel us. Just not good enough. We need to get better. In all areas.
“It starts now for everybody in this organization. Assess the year and come back and be better next year, because it wasn’t good enough.”
In the wake of such disappointment, there’s one overarching question: How does this not happen again?
It’s been back-to-back years of this, the Cubs dispatched by the rival Brewers in the NLDS a year ago. That was described as fuel for their fire this season, but the embers didn’t even burn long enough for a rematch.
Craig Counsell, whom the Cubs poached from those Brewers, has two early postseason exits in three seasons at the helm, with two years left on the contract that made him the game’s highest-paid skipper.
“We lost,” Counsell said. “There’s a response to it that we get to choose, and we’ve got to improve. Everybody can point at themselves and say, ‘We’ve got to get a little bit better.’
“We’re going to have to wait to accomplish the thing we really want to accomplish. … We didn’t finish it this year, and you hope that this has to be part of the journey to the ultimate prize.”
With the investments made in Counsell, Bregman, Crow-Armstrong and more, the expectations are not going to change. The Cubs will head into next season thinking World Series, just like this year.
But at least at the moment, they have a lot of questions to answer about how they’re going to get there.
What will make the 2027 group better equipped than the 2026 one?
That’s what the offseason — likely to be halted by a lengthy work stoppage — will teach us.
This was a roller-coaster campaign, with high highs and low lows, a lot of pitching injuries and a final-week downturn that came at exactly the wrong time.
The thoughts on the minds of everyone inside the losing clubhouse Wednesday were of further blows this team is about to take, the players who aren’t going to return, the pending free agents who were such a part of this group and its plan to deliver on those championship-level expectations.
“We’ll talk about the baseball plenty,” second baseman Nico Hoerner said, “but when you get through a locker room with people that you’re really close with and people that aren’t guaranteed to come back here — and not seeing this thing through the way a lot of us envisioned and believed in — that’s the stuff that doesn’t sit right and hurts.”
Perhaps most important for Jed Hoyer’s front office, the Cubs might have to replace their entire starting rotation, with lefties Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga and David Peterson, plus righties Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman, all set to hit free agency.
Righties Cade Horton, Edward Cabrera and Ben Brown, plus lefty Justin Steele, make for an intriguing group of possible replacements, but all are coming off injuries, a risky play.
Then there’s the corner outfielders.
Right fielder Seiya Suzuki has been an offensive force it will be tough for the Cubs to replace; he’s expected to be one of the best hitters on the market and land a big contract.
Left fielder Ian Happ is a franchise fixture whose potential departure had teammates crying Wednesday night.
“He embodies the Cubs more than anyone I know,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said through tears.
Sentimentality is a rare reason to spend for baseball front offices. Happ didn’t have the type of offensive season he consistently has throughout his career though still played excellent defense and hit for power.
“All I can say is that I love being a Cub,” Happ said. “I’ve loved my time. I’ve loved the place, the people, Wrigley Field, the fan base. And it’s been truly special. I don’t think there’s a better place in baseball to play.”
With decisions to make, how Hoyer crafts his roster – and how these Cubs respond to another bout of playoff disappointment – will answer that overarching question, the only question that matters:
How do the Cubs make sure this doesn’t happen again?

パドレスに連敗しポストシーズン敗退となったカブス。試合後に今永昇太投手が今季、苦戦するなかで、鈴木誠也選手のアドバイスで活路を見い出した事実があったことを明かしました。
ポストシーズン敗退が決定し、試合後にインタビューに応じた今永昇太投手。登板できず今季を終えてしまったことに悔しさをにじませるなか、3年間チームメートとして過ごした鈴木選手について話題が及びます。
今永投手はメジャー挑戦1年目から、鈴木選手の支えがあったと語り、さらに「本当にこれ冗談抜きで今年の5月、6月よくなっていったところは、鈴木選手からアドバイスをもらった、ここではちょっと言えないですけど、バッターからの目線でアドバイスをもらった部分が大きかったので、やっぱりこのメジャーの世界ってデータが主流とか今、言われていますけど、僕はずっとこの2年間、ピッチャーから見た一方通行のデータしか見ていなかったので、バッターから自分を見た時にどうなのかというのは、あまり参考にしなかったというか、そういうデータをもらったりもしなかったので、バッターがどうされたら嫌なのかというのを、そういうヒントを与えてくれた存在なので、ものすごく感謝していますね」と述べ、アドバイスをきっかけに状態が好転したことを明かしました。

The San Diego Padres blitzed the Chicago Cubs in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card series, 8-0, to put themselves one win away from a date with the Milwaukee Brewers in the NLDS. Plenty of Padres deserve credit for Tuesday night's dominant performance, but none more than soon-to-be-free agent Michael King.
San Diego's ace put together one of the best postseason starts in recent memory, carrying a no-hitter into the seventh inning. He finished with seven scoreless frames, allowing one hit, three walks and recording eight strikeouts. As Padres fans celebrate King's masterclass, prospective free agency suitors are chomping at the bit. Here are a few potential landing spots:
Atlanta Braves
The Braves rotation is a bit scarce behind Chris Sale. Tyler Mahle has eviscerated the competition since arriving at the trade deadline, but he's a free agent next winter. AJ Smith-Shawver, J.R. Ritchie and Owen Murphy are all exciting young arms, but it's unclear which of them will click as full-time starters — and how soon. Martín Pérez, one of this season's great surprises for Atlanta, is also an upcoming free agent.
Atlanta doesn't typically pay sticker price on free agent pitchers but there is immense pressure to compete now — right now — in the twilight years of Sale's career. He won't be able to anchor this rotation forever and the Braves need to start hedging their bets, just in case Father Time catches up.
King, with a 3.21 ERA and 1.18 WHIP, has made 32 starts and pitched a career-high 185 innings this season. The Braves need depth and dependability most desperately, and that's something King can provide. It doesn't hurt that he is building a nice postseason résumé for himself.
Baltimore Orioles
Every winter, we all wonder if Baltimore might finally upgrade its pitching staff. The Corbin Burnes era burned bright and fast. Shane Baz was a savvy trade addition last winter, but the Orioles still struggled to field five quality, healthy starters for the 162-game duration of the regular season.
Trevor Rogers, their best pitcher two years running, will now enter free agency. That leaves Baltimore's front office will a clear and immediate need in the rotation. It seems like the O's new ownership group will, on some level, spend more than the previous administration. The Pete Alonso signing was a stark departure from business as usual in Baltimore. As such, it's not hard to envision the O's ponying up for a second-tier ace like Michael King; the Tarik Skubals of the world are still outside their price range, no doubt.
If Kyle Bradish can finally get healthy for a year, and if the O's deign to re-sign Rogers (or pursue another mid-rotation arm in addition to King), this rotation could shape up quite nicely. Baltimore has the offensive firepower to compete in the AL East. King can help round out a postseason-caliber roster.
Toronto Blue Jays
A nightmare Blue Jays season has finally come to an end, but Toronto should be right back in the postseason fray next season with better luck and an productive winter. The Jays front office is probably the most aggressive in baseball outside of L.A. or New York.
Last offseason, their big fish was Dylan Cease, who immediately turned in a Cy Young-caliber campaign. At the trade deadline, Toronto did not strictly sell, despite sitting near the bottom of the standings. The Jays went out and added José Soriano, another frontline starter at the peak of his powers.
Toronto can expect a healtheir Trey Yesavage in 2027, too, so a premium free agent addition (like King) could quickly transform the Blue Jays rotation into one of the deepest and most fearsome in the American League. If Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and Toronto's boppers put their best foot forward, there's no reason Toronto can't win the division and compete (again) for a World Series.
Houston Astros
The Astros went bullpen against bullpen in their AL Wild Card series opener against the White Sox. Houston was lucky Chicago only managed six runs, with many, many base-runners stranded in scoring position. That did not mean much for the Astros, unfortunately, as the Chicago bullpen — against all odds — mostly kept a more seasoned Houston lineup in check.
Houston has a proper 1A ace in Hunter Brown, but the rotation behind him is total patchwork. Peter Lambert put together a solid campaign and Ethan Pecko faired well in his first taste of MLB action, but the Astros can't really trust anyone besides Brown. Tatsuya Imai, their prized free agent addition last winter, was little more than a bulk reliever in his rookie season.
The Astros have gotten cheaper and cheaper in recent years and the results are getting worse and worse, predictably. Still, this core has competed for a World Series in the not-so-distant past, and we know ownership is capable of spending at the upper echelon of free agency. King would do a lot to solidify the Astros' pitching plans in 2027.
Chicago Cubs
Injuries decimated the Cubs rotation this season. Justin Steele, Cade Horton and Ben Brown should all return in 2027, which is a major, natural influx of talent. If Edward Cabrera can rebound, the Cubs rotation will be all rainbows and sunshine — at least on paper.
But as this season once again reminded us, what happens "on paper" almost never translates to reality. Shōta Imanaga and Matthew Boyd are both upcoming free agents. Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes, Chicago's emergency deadline rentals, are also halfway out the door. There's uncertainty around how exactly the likes of Steele and Horton will perform coming off of major elbow surgeries, too. So the Cubs should play it safe and hyper-focus on pitching depth.
The rotation could be what sends Chicago home against San Diego. So, why not use the Padres own weapons against them in free agency and sign King? "Stability" is a word that comes to mind with King, and that's exactly what the Cubs need right now.

item.content:encoded:
The MLB playoffs are here as 12 teams survived the regular season and are ready for an all-out battle for October supremacy. Each of the remaining squads has spent the last six months proving it belonged in the postseason. None of the last teams standing got here unscathed and all have glaring weaknesses that could end their seasons early.
With postseason baseball upon us, here is the fatal flaw that could derail each MLB playoff team.
Brewers: Lack of Power
The Brewers were baseball’s best team all season but that doesn’t mean they’re perfect. Milwaukee has a great rotation fronted by baseball’s new ace Jacob Misiorowski, and a good bullpen, but the lineup relies heavily on getting hits up and down the lineup. The Brewers play the 2026 version of small ball, and don’t have a ton of power. That can kill teams in October, when runs come at a premium.
Milwaukee finished the season tied for 28th in home runs (154) and 25th in isolated power (.144). The Brewers were tied for 10th in slugging (.403) and were third in wRC+ (107), but the lack of top-line power could be their downfall. Against elite pitching in the postseason, it’s much more difficult to string together hits and build big innings. Being able to get runs on balls that leave the yard is huge. Each of the last six World Series champions ranked inside the top five in regular season home runs.
Maybe Milwaukee bucks that trend, but if they don’t win the World Series, a lack of power may be the reason.
Dodgers: Health
The Dodgers have won two straight titles and at full strength, they’d be the overwhelming favorite to take home a third in a row. But L.A. has dealt with major injuries all season and the team looks more vulnerable than it has in a long time as we enter the postseason.
Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow combined to make only 22 starts this season. Both are back now, but neither has been particularly reliable—Snell left his penultimate start on Sept. 16 with a groin injury before returning to pitch four innings on Saturday. Tarik Skubal had elbow surgery earlier this year with the Tigers and hasn’t been quite as dominant as usual when it comes to limiting baserunners. Shohei Ohtani has been sidelined by knee and biceps injuries, and won’t be pitching in October. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernandez are showing signs of decline and have played a ton of baseball over the last three years.
L.A. is still loaded, but a few injuries to a roster that’s had its fair share of medical issues could make things dicey.
Rays: Trouble Against Lefties
It’s hard to find too many flaws here. The Rays are an incredibly balanced squad that was the best in the AL pretty much all season. One of the only red flags here is the team’s performance against lefties, and they’re likely to run into a few in the playoffs.
Against lefties as a team, Tampa Bay ranked 27th in slugging (.364), 26th in wRC+ (90) and 25th in OPS (.679). Luckily for the Rays, their best offensive players hammered lefties. Junior Caminero slashed .287/.426/.490 with eight home runs and a 152 wRC+. Unfortunately, the 23-year-old and Yandy Diaz are the team’s only players who appeared in 100-plus games and topped .700 in OPS against lefties.
That’s a weakness opponents will try to exploit in October. The Rays don’t have many holes, but good left-handed pitching could be the kryptonite that slows one of baseball’s most complete teams.
Braves: A Hole at Shortstop
The Braves have plenty of star power in the lineup and Chris Sale at the top of their rotation but they have a huge flaw at the heart of their team. Atlanta’s shortstops were among the worst offensively during the 2026 season. Ha-seong Kim is is the starter, but he had a .359 OPS with zero home runs in 147 plate appearances this season so I’m not sure that is the answer. The other option is Mauricio Dubón, who had a .719 OPS in 153 games, but that won’t work against southpaws since it means lefty Mike Yastrzemski must play left field.
Collectively, Braves shortstops slashed .241/.295/.349 during the regular season and ranked 27th with a wRC+ of 78. They also ranked 23rd in fWAR (1.6) and bWAR (-0.4). They simply haven’t gotten enough out of the position and need to find some offensive production there.
Atlanta went wire-to-wire to win the NL East and did so while not getting much from a premium position. Against elite pitching in the postseason, they’ll need production out of everyone in the lineup at some point. Carrying an empty spot will likely prove to be more damaging than it already has been.
Yankees: An Aaron Judge-Sized Hole in the Lineup
The Yankees may have baseball’s best postseason rotation and found enough offense to hold onto the AL’s top wild-card spot. But to win a World Series, they need their best player healthy and hammering baseballs. They may not have it.
Aaron Judge is trying to return for the wild-card series from a strained calf muscle, but it would be unwise to rush him back into action. Yes, New York needs his bat in the lineup, but it also needs to ensure he is available for the entire postseason, not just the first series. Ben Rice (149), Cody Bellinger (115) and Paul Goldschmidt (111) are the only Yankees with more than 300 plate appearances and a wRC+ over 100. That’s a scary lack of production from the lineup.
They need Judge’s bat back at full health as soon as possible simply because the team relies on him so much to produce.
Padres: Who Starts After Michael King?
The Padres have baseball’s best bullpen and an offense that has been clicking on all cylinders in the second half. What they don’t have is a deep rotation after injuries have decimated it.
Michael King is the team’s ace and should be reliable in that spot, but after him things get dicey. Nick Pivetta missed most of the season due to a flexor strain in his pitching elbow that cost him nearly five months. He’s back and has thrown well, but he’s only made eight starts this year. After that, it’ll be some combination of Robbie Ray and Walker Buehler. Both have been up and down this season and neither feels like a rock-solid option.
If San Diego can get decent starts and shorten games by getting the bullpen in early, things could be fine. But if the team’s starters struggle it could mean an early exit.
Cubs: A Battered Starting Rotation
The Cubs have one of baseball’s best offenses and its best all-around player in Pete Crow-Armstrong, but their pitching staff remains a patchwork mess. The team’s starting rotation has endured season-ending injuries to Cade Horton and Ben Brown, Justin Steele still hasn’t returned after elbow surgery in 2025, Matthew Boyd missed time thanks to knee surgery and a shoulder issue, and Kevin Gausman is now dealing with a shoulder injury.
Chicago will open the postseason with Boyd on the mound and should follow with Clay Holmes in Game 2, then Shota Imanaga and, if he’s healthy enough, Gausman. How bad has it been for the Cubs? Among starters, only Imanaga generated 2.0 bWAR this year. That’s a dangerous weakness to carry into the postseason when pitching becomes even more important.
Could the Cubs manage to overcome a rotation that has been battered all season? It’s possible, but that would take a herculean effort from the team’s top-ranked offense.
Phillies: Trea Turner’s Disappearing Production
Trea Turner was a key piece of the Phillies’ success in 2025, as he slashed .302/.354/.450 with 15 home runs, 36 stolen bases and a 123 wRC+ in 141 games. The team is probably wondering where that guy went.
In 157 games this year, Turner slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs, 21 stolen bases and a wRC+ of 83. His strikeout rate jumped from 16.7% to 21.0%, his xBA dropped from .270 to .242 and his xwOBA of .293 ranked in the 14th percentile. That would be manageable if Turner provided value defensively, but his outs above average dropped from 17 in 2025 to -8 this season. That’s a precipitous, ominous drop for a shortstop who’s in his age-33 season, has always depended on his athleticism and still has seven more years on his contract. Philadelphia has underachieved as a whole in 2026, and Turner is the poster child.
While he was a disappointment in the regular season, Turner has a ton of playoff experience and won a title with the Nationals in 2019. Maybe he’ll turn it around when the lights are the brightest. But his postseason track record doesn’t offer much optimism. He has a career playoff OPS of .681.
Red Sox: A Top-Heavy Offense
Boston’s comeback story this season was remarkable after Alex Cora was fired following a 10–17 start. While they were one of MLB’s best teams over the final two-thirds of the season, the offense never really clicked one through nine. As a team, the Red Sox finished 17th in wRC+ (99) and 19th in OPS (.717). And it seemed all season a few guys would come through, while the rest of the lineup struggled.
Among the team’s hitters who played at least 100 games, only Willson Contreras (151), Wilyer Abreu (112) and Ceddanne Rafaela (109) topped 100 in wRC+ to grade out as above-average hitters. The drop-off from Contreras to the rest of the roster is pretty alarming in itself, though Mickey Gasper (130), Masataka Yoshida (108) and Roman Anthony (106) all performed well in fewer than 300 plate appearances. Key pieces like Caleb Durbin (100) and especially Jarren Duran (69) had off years, while catcher Adley Rutschman slashed .222/.278/.410 with a wRC+ of 88 after arriving at the trade deadline.
Boston will have to overcome those issues throughout the lineup, particularly against the kind of pitching ahead in the postseason. The lack of offensive balance could be the team’s downfall.
Guardians: A Lineup Short of Firepower
The Guardians are in an enviable position, as they barely made the playoffs but wound up with the AL’s No. 2 seed. While they are set up for success thanks to the bracket and have an excellent pitching staff, their lineup has been anemic.
Cleveland finished the regular season ranked 27th in home runs (162) and slugging (.380), 26th in OPS (.696), 24th in runs scored (678) and 21st in wRC+ (97). Meanwhile, star third baseman José Ramírez wrapped up the worst full season of his career, slashing .235/.320/.368 with 12 home runs and a wRC+ of 92. The question is simple: Where do the runs come from? Rookie Chase DeLauter was the team’s most productive hitter after slashing .287/.363/.456 with 16 home runs and a 131 wRC+, but he doesn't have much help. Steven Kwan was second on the team in wRC+ (114), but only slugged .349, while Travis Bazzana (110) and Angel Martinez (108) were both only modestly above average by wRC+. The rest of the lineup struggled to generate offense.
After a tough battle down the stretch, the Guardians wound up with a favorable path in the postseason. But getting to the World Series will likely require unearthing some unsung heroes on offense.
White Sox: October Inexperience
The White Sox surprised everyone with their run to a postseason berth after three consecutive 100-loss seasons. The roster has been properly overhauled, with only 19.8% of the team’s plate appearances coming from players on the 121-loss team in 2024. The problem is, most of the team’s new players have little to no postseason experience.
Braden Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Sam Antonacci are rookies, while Colson Montgomery, Kyle Teel, Chase Meidroth and Grant Taylor are second-year players. Sean Burke debuted in 2024, but has never pitched in the postseason, and All-Star Miguel Vargas has likewise never appeared in the postseason despite coming up with the Dodgers. Maybe there’s something to be said for youthful exuberance, but there’s also the possibility that fatigue becomes a factor for players who haven’t been through a playoff chase before. Colson Montgomery posted a wRC+ of 54 after August 1, while Murakami slashed .156/.299/.375 in that stretch.
Chicago is built for success long-term, but its lack of postseason experience could be a significant obstacle in October.
Astros: A Thin Starting Rotation
The Astros finished 81–81 to win the weak AL West and notch a playoff spot. Given their record, it’s not surprising they have a ton of issues across the roster. The most glaring is their starting rotation, which is in rough shape.
Beyond Hunter Brown, Houston simply doesn’t have the kind of high-end starting pitching that wins in October. And even Brown enters the playoffs with some uncertainty, having thrown only 107 ⅓ innings this season after missing a chunk of the campaign with a shoulder injury. Peter Lambert has become the team’s No. 2 starter, but he went 8–10 with a 3.82 ERA and doesn’t possess premium stuff. Hayden Wesneski finished the season strong, but made only 11 starts all year, while Cristian Javier and Mike Burrows are both on the IL.
The rotation is so thin that the Astros are poised to open Game 1 of the wild-card series with a bullpen game to give Brown, Lambert and Wesneski rest. It’s hardly an ideal situation and there aren’t many options available for manager Joe Espada.

SAN DIEGO — The Chicago Cubs are again turning to left-hander Matthew Boyd to begin their postseason.
Boyd, who got the Game 1 start in last year’s wild-card series against the San Diego Padres, will again get the ball when the Cubs open their rematch Tuesday, this time at Petco Park. The Cubs also could have started right-hander Kevin Gausman but opted for the lefty. Boyd held the Padres to one run in 4 1/3 innings in Game 1 last season at Wrigley Field.
“The first two months of the season were certainly interrupted and not smooth, but since then he’s gotten into a routine and consistency, that is what I think Matthew offers,” manager Craig Counsell said Monday after their team workout. “Playoff starts are a challenge. Matthew’s experienced in that and had good experiences last year with it for us and look for him to do the same tomorrow.”
Since returning from meniscus surgery June 25, Boyd posted a 3.42 ERA in his final 17 starts, allowing three earned runs or fewer in 12 of those outings.
Counsell didn’t provide specifics on who could start Games 2 or 3, the latter if necessary Thursday. Gausman is expected to pitch at some point in the series. His left shoulder injury sustained in his final regular-season start Wednesday created some uncertainty about whether he would be available this playoff round. The Cubs feel Gausman’s shoulder is trending well but isn’t fully in the clear, making a Tuesday start not a realistic option.
The Cubs are expected to carry 12 pitchers on their wild-card roster. Left-hander Shota Imanaga is also expected to factor into the Cubs’ pitching plans this series, though Counsell cautioned he didn’t know whether that would be as a starter or a reliever. Right-hander Clay Holmes wasn’t at his best down the stretch, but the Cubs anticipate him providing bulk in some capacity this series, whether that’s in a start or multiple innings out of the bullpen.
The best-of-three series allows Counsell to fully deploy all his pitchers as needed, whether it’s using starters out of the bullpen for multiple frames or even one-inning appearances. The Cubs will seek the best matchups and pockets of hitters for their pitchers to face.
“I look at these games kind of in this context that we’re talking about the urgency is you have 27 outs, we’ve got to figure out how to get 27 outs,” Counsell said. “The order that that happens — starter, reliever, closer, setup man — those words don’t matter. We’re just trying to get 27 outs.”
The Cubs’ pitching plans beyond Game 1 will be dictated by whether they win or lose the opener. It’ll be all hands on deck Wednesday for Game 2 if they don’t pull out the win Tuesday.
“It doesn’t matter how anything happens tomorrow, like aesthetically, it just matters that we win, that’s the bottom line,” Counsell said. “Because we’ve got to win two games in the next three days and so how anybody does, how anything happens, it doesn’t matter. You’ve got to win the game. And I think you probably lean more on the process over 162 games because you have to. But when you get to a two-out-of-three series to play the next game, your thoughts have to change a little bit.”
In a rematch of last year’s wild-card matchup, a venue change presents an added challenge for the Cubs against a Padres team with one of the best home records in baseball — 51-30 at Petco Park this year compared to 40-41 on the road.
The Cubs haven’t decided yet whether Alex Bregman is feeling well enough to start at third base or if they keep using him as the designated hitter to reduce the risk as he continues to play with multiple facial fractures. He took grounders at third base during live batting practice Monday, an encouraging development.
Bregman’s quick return gives the Cubs’ lineup added juice.
“I definitely think that fires you up,” Pete Crow-Armstrong said Monday. “Knowing him and how wonderfully crazed he is just about his work and how much he loves the game, not really surprising. Not to put a damper on how cool it is that he is coming back after eight facial fractures and whatnot, like, I’m just not surprised. He lives for this kind of baseball.”
