item.content:encoded:
The best time of the baseball year is finally here. The playoffs begin Tuesday, with a quadruple-header of wild-card games on tap. The schedule for each series' first two games is identical.
Let's break down how each team got here, how they can win, X-factors, series predictions and more before the wild-card round begins.
AL: CWS-HOU • BOS-NYY | NL: PHI-ATL • CHC-SD
No. 6 Philadelphia Phillies vs. No. 3 Atlanta Braves
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 2 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Jesús Luzardo (PHI) vs. Chris Sale (ATL)
Game 2, 2 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Cristopher Sánchez (PHI) vs. Tyler Mahle (ATL)
Game 3, TBD*: Aaron Nola (or Zack Wheeler on four days' rest) (PHI) vs. Grant Holmes (ATL)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Phillies: It was a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde type of season for the Phillies, to say the least. For the second time in five seasons, an in-season managerial firing was needed to light a fire under an underperforming veteran roster that appeared to be letting their window close. But the Phillies, like they've done before, found a way to get themselves going on the back of their starting rotation. The Phillies didn't make it easy on themselves in September, going 10-14 down the stretch and needing to win their regular-season finale against the Rays to punch their ticket to the postseason. But now that they're in, this veteran group will look to show that they're better than the past month suggests.
Braves: It was a reassuring year in Atlanta, a much-needed reminder that no, this era of Braves baseball was not over after their disastrous, postseason-less 2025. A change in manager, from the now-retired Brian Snitker to the endearingly pugnacious Walt Weiss, set the tone. As did a major refresh of Atlanta's coaching staff. That turnover, in contrast with the continuity on the roster, proved crucial as Atlanta waltzed to its first division title since 2023.
Big campaigns from metronomic first baseman Matt Olson and 2025 NL Rookie of the Year Drake Baldwin shocked nobody. The same was true for ace Chris Sale, certain to be voted an NL Cy Young finalist. But few would've predicted Michael Harris II leading the team in bWAR with a dynamic, consistent offensive season. Role players such as Mauricio Dubón, Mike Yastrzemski and Dominic Smith all delivered critical production to help offset underwhelming seasons from the likes of Ozzie Albies and Austin Riley.
Ronald Acuña Jr., that wonderfully mercurial burst of baseballing light, might've fit into that last group if not for an otherworldly September in which he clocked seven homers with a .950 OPS. That renaissance continuing into October would be a game-changer for the Braves, whose 2021 title came with Acuña sidelined.
X-factors
Phillies: Trea Turner
The regular season wasn't kind to shortstop Trea Turner, who recorded the worst season of his career. But the thing about the postseason is that it allows players who have not yet written the final story on their season to become heroes. And if the Phillies want to move past Atlanta and reach the NLDS for the fifth straight year, Turner finding his rhythm would be a welcomed sight for the team's offense. Turner has a .733 OPS off Sale in 25 career at-bats and a very respectable .863 OPS off Mahle in 25 career at-bats.
Braves: Tyler Mahle
Chris Sale is going to start Game 1 for Atlanta, and he's probably going to be pretty good. That feels as bankable as anything in our topsy-turvy world. But Mahle, set to throw Game 2, has been one of the game's most reliable starters since he joined the Braves from a zip-less San Francisco team at the deadline. The veteran righty posted a 1.99 ERA with Atlanta, allowing one earned or fewer in seven of his nine starts.
Mahle's most recent start, however, was a relative stinker. He surrendered five runs and struck out just four at home against an undermanned Reds lineup. And the underlying metrics, it should be said, are a bit more skeptical about Mahle's prospects. That's understandable. He doesn't throw that hard or strike out oodles of hitters. He hasn't conjured more swing-and-miss or meaningfully lowered opponents' hard-hit rate as a Brave. And yet, Mahle has found a way to find outs. Whether he can do so against Philly's bats will be huge.
How they win
Phillies: Can any team in baseball go toe-to-toe with Philly's starting rotation? With the quartet of Wheeler, Sánchez, Luzardo and Nola, the Phillies should have the advantage in a three-, five- or seven-game series. So while their offense is more of a wild card (pun intended), this team should be able to count on its starter giving them a chance to win every time out. And if that foursome gets hot, it's not outlandish to believe they could carry Philly on another deep postseason run.
Braves: It has been a restful week for the Braves, who were able to sit back, relax and line up their starting rotation for this wild-card series. The same cannot be said for Philly, which needed every last out to clinch on the regular season's final day. For the Phillies, the sense of exhaustion is real and gives Atlanta a legitimate advantage.
But it all starts with Sale. If he cruises like he's capable of in Game 1, that puts Atlanta in the catbird seat. Only one team in the current playoff format (the 2025 Yankees) came back to win a wild-card series after losing the first game.
Series prediction: Braves in 3
No. 6 Chicago White Sox vs. No. 3 Houston Astros
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 5 p.m. ET Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): David Sandlin (CWS) vs. Peter Lambert (HOU)
Game 2 5 p.m. ET Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Sean Burke (CWS) vs. Hunter Brown (HOU)
Game 3, TBD*: Davis Martin (CWS) vs. Hayden Wesneski (HOU)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
White Sox: The White Sox have been easily one of the best stories of the 2026 regular season, reaching the postseason for the first time since 2021. Chicago became the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason following three consecutive 100-loss seasons, capturing the third AL wild-card spot. The offense, led by first-time All-Stars Miguel Vargas and Munetaka Murakami, was the driving force behind the Sox's success. Chicago finished the season with a top-five offense in MLB.
The fact that the White Sox didn't win the AL Central might come as a disappointment, considering they were in first place for the majority of the second half. Still, it's undeniable that any result that puts them in the playoffs is a huge victory for the organization and a fan base that has been waiting for competitive baseball.
Astros: For a franchise that has accomplished so much over the past decade, there's something shameful, even humiliating about raising the 2026 AL West banner. That's because these Astros are, by record, the single worst division winner in the sport's long past. Before Sunday, no team with a .500 record or below had ever reached the postseason. But Houston rewrote history thanks to an MVP-caliber season from Yordan Alvarez and a tidal wave of mediocrity from its AL West counterparts. Their inclusion in the October jamboree is more an indictment of the Texas Rangers and the Seattle Mariners than anything else, but the Astros at least ended on a high note with their 9-0 win over the A's on Sunday.
Houston also deserves a morsel of credit for refurbishing its season after a disastrous April. Reaching .500 with the fourth-worst starting staff by ERA — only the Reds, A's and Rockies were worse — is also an accomplishment worth commending, a testament to something. Where would this club be without Peter Lambert, whose 3.87 ERA in 153 2/3 innings offered the only semblance of stability for a roster constantly in flux?
Things got sad enough, discombobulated enough, that in August owner Jim Crane relieved GM Dana Brown of his duties. There's an overwhelming expectation that skipper Joe Espada won't be back next year, either. It's difficult to be optimistic about Houston's very uncertain future. But in the random present of playoff baseball, anything is possible — especially when you employ the best hitter on the planet.
X-factors
White Sox: Munetaka Murakami
Munetaka Murakami is a game-changer, and his presence in the White Sox's lineup is a huge advantage in the postseason. The White Sox's rookie slugger burst onto the scene in 2026, hitting 35 home runs and providing instant impact in his first season after coming over from Japan. But following a midseason hamstring injury, the league seemed to adjust to him; Murakami finished with a slashline of .184/.328/.423 and 11 homers since Aug 1. Still, he has the type of power that can change a series by himself, and with three homers in the final week of the season, he appears to be coming out of his second-half slump. If Murakami has rediscovered his power stroke, it could change this series.
Astros: Isaac Paredes
Yordan Alvarez is currently the best hitter on earth. He cannot, under any circumstances, be allowed to dictate proceedings during this series. Chicago must make somebody else in Houston's mediocre lineup beat them. If there's a base open with Alvarez up, he should just stroll straight to first every time.
That puts a mountain of pressure on Paredes. The stocky third baseman has been hitting right behind Alvarez for most of the season and has, for the most part, showed well. He's a supremely weird hitter, one who rarely hits the ball hard or barrels it up. But Paredes doesn't whiff, doesn't punch out and has a preternatural knack for pulling the ball in the air. Expect him to come up multiple times in big spots with runners on.
How they win
White Sox: The White Sox's offense has carried them all season, and if they hope to advance to the ALDS against their division rival, they'll have to slug their way there. Vargas, Murakami and shortstop Colson Montgomery each finished the season with more than 30 longballs, and the Sox finished fifth in MLB in homers. For a team built to slug, Daikin Park in Houston isn't the worst environment to play in on the road. Chicago's power-packed lineup has shown that if they're hitting the ball out of the ballpark, offensively, they can play with anyone.
Astros: Houston desperately needs offensive contributions from someone besides Alvarez. Maybe it's the aforementioned Paredes or the en fuego Yainer Díaz. Perhaps Jose Altuve, 36 years old and in full decline, has one magical month left in his Hall of Fame career. But with such a tattered pitching staff, the Astros need to score to win. They also need to win the Hunter Brown start; he's far and away their best starter. They need a lot, frankly. And yet, much weirder October things have happened inside that East Texas thunderdome over the past decade.
Series prediction: Astros in 3
No. 5 Boston Red Sox vs. No. 4 New York Yankees
Projected starters
(all times ET)
Game 1, 8 p.m. Tuesday (NBC/PCK): Payton Tolle (BOS) vs. Cam Schlittler (NYY)
Game 2, 8 p.m. Wednesday (NBC/PCK): Sonny Gray (BOS) vs. Max Fried (NYY)
Game 3, TBD*: Ranger Suárez (BOS) vs. Gerrit Cole (NYY)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Red Sox: Odysseus would be proud. What a winding, bizarre and tumultuous road it has been for the Sox. Boston began the year like a snail on Unisom, posting a lackluster 9-17 record through April 24. That precipitated a dramatic, Red Wedding-style culling, in which manager Alex Cora and several other staff members were relieved of their duties. Extended injury list stints for the team's two most important pieces, outfielder Roman Anthony and 2025 Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, made a turnaround feel awfully unlikely. On July 24, the Sox lost a rubber match in Colorado and traveled home 14 games under .500. Their postseason odds wallowed around 10%.
Then, everything changed. It began with a home mop against the Yanks and fully kicked into gear when the Red Sox hit the road for a three-city swing the first week of July. They went 9-0 on that trip before winning six straight at home. That 15-game streak catapulted them back into contention and the good graces of an understandably unplugged fan base. Between July 3 and Aug. 7, the Sox went a ridiculous 32-5, trampolining from 14 games under .500 to 13 games over. Fenway was a zoo. Nothing could go wrong. Boston ballfans beamed once again.
The heater earned Cora's replacement, Chad Tracy, the full-time gig. It also afforded the Sox a relatively comfortable September. It's worth noting, though, that Boston has not played particularly crisply since cooling off from the volcanic run, with a 21-22 record since Aug. 8. Ultimately, their final numbers and standing in the American League are not shocking or unexpected, even though Boston's odyssey was wonky beyond comparison.
Yankees: For all the stress, the drama, the hand-wringing, for all the injuries and under-performance, 2026 was a relatively straightforward season in YankeeLand. A lot, it should be said, went wrong. Reigning AL MVP Aaron Judge has played just seven games since May. Giancarlo Stanton hasn't played since April. Max Fried and Carlos Rodón each missed about two months. Young players such as Anthony Volpe, Jasson Dominguez and Austin Wells regressed offensively. Gerrit Cole, coming back from Tommy John, didn't fully recapture his frontline best.
And yet, here the Yankees are, with 93 wins and in an identical place to where they finished last year. That's thanks to breakout campaigns from homegrown pieces such as Cam Schlittler (the AL Cy Young favorite) and Ben Rice (41 home runs and a .897 OPS). Closer David Bednar has been dynamite. Cody Bellinger has been a rock. Skipper Aaron Boone kept the train on the tracks. Three games at home against the Red Sox await. Beyond that looms an ALDS against a daunting division foe. We've been here before.
The largest difference, of course, is the uncertainty swirling around Judge. The Yankees' captain missed three months due to a rib problem, came back for a week, strained his calf and went back on the shelf. Boone says he's preparing for a wild-card round without Judge. Judge says he plans to play. What sort of magic this reduced version of Judge can conjure is easily the juiciest storyline ahead of this rivalry showdown. That said, this series, like this Yankees season, is probably going to be dictated by the pitchers.
X-factors
Red Sox: Roman Anthony
It has been an odd season for the 22-year-old, who missed last year's wild-card festivities due to injury. In March, Anthony was a late addition to Team USA's WBC roster. He shined on that grand stage, impressing his more established teammates and earning plaudits from a coaching staff of hardball lifers. That only ratcheted up the hype on a player expected to carry a franchise less than a year after he became legally permitted to drink a beer.
So when Anthony started slowly, disappointment bubbled. Then, on May 4, he tore a ligament in his finger; that kept him out of action until Aug. 30. A lot happened in the interim, most of which Anthony spent rehabbing at the team's complex in Florida. Since returning, he has looked promising, tantalizingly close to unleashing the full assortment of his talents upon the league. Now, with Willson Contreras banged up and either unavailable or restricted, the pressure returns to Anthony's young shoulders.
Yankees: Luis García Jr.
García was a curious character for the Yankees to shape their trade deadline around. Instead of acquiring a piece that filled an obvious void (righty stick with defensive value or versatility), GM Brian Cashman opted to add the most dynamic hitter possible. New York landed on García, who was in the midst of an offensive breakout under a new Washington Nationals regime.
For a month, that plan bore fruit, with the Dominican slugger posting an .846 OPS in August. But since then, the wheels have fallen off, with García's chase rate skyrocketing. His September OPS started with a 5. He has homered just twice since Aug. 26. He doesn't have an extra-base hit since Sept. 10. There's a chance, given Boston's bevy of southpaws and New York's DH surplus, that he doesn't start every game. But García will get his chances, and whether he comes up big might swing the series.
How they win
Red Sox: Boston's pitching staff is the only one in baseball that ranks in the top five in both home run rate and walk rate. That's a rare combo. Usually, throwing the ball in the strike zone more often leads to more hard contact. But these Red Sox hurlers, for whatever reason, have threaded that needle perfectly. No team in the league has allowed fewer homers. However, no team has hit more than the Yankees. Boston revitalized its season behind pitching and defense, keeping the scores low and the games close. Doing so here will give them the best chance of authoring an upset.
Yankees: No American League team can compete with New York's starting staff. But the Yankees need more than dominance from Schlittler, Fried and Cole. They need length. The bridge to Bednar is unsteady. So the longer the starters go, the rosier that path looks. Offensively, the Yankees need a big swing or two from their right-handed bats against Boston's left-handed arms. That could come from a banged-up Judge or Stanton. It could come from veteran southpaw-killer Paul Goldschmidt, trade-acquisition Heliot Ramos or rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. If it comes from the beleaguered Anthony Volpe, the tri-state area will lose its collective marbles. But somebody, anybody who stands on the right side of the batter's box has to make an impact.
Series prediction: Yankees in 3
No. 5 Chicago Cubs vs. No. 4 San Diego Padres
(all times ET)
Projected starters
Game 1, 10 p.m. Tuesday (PCK/NBCSN): Shota Imanaga (CHC) vs. Michael King (SD)
Game 2, 10 p.m. Wednesday (PCK/NBCSN): Clay Holmes (CHC) vs. Nick Pivetta (SD)
Game 3, TBD*: Matthew Boyd (CHC) vs. Walker Buehler or Casey Mize or Robbie Ray (SD)
(*if necessary)
How they got here
Cubs: It was Pete Crow-Armstrong's world, and the rest of us just lived in it. Chicago's 24-year-old center fielder went fully supersonic this year, cranking 45 homers, swiping 41 bags and delivering a .945 OPS with his typically elite outfield defense. He will win the NL MVP, and it might be unanimous. That performance shaped and guided and defined this Cubs' season, electrifying an offense that led baseball in OPS, K/BB rate and runs per game.
Alex Bregman's arrival via free agency, too, cannot be understated. He struggled mightily for the first few months, with his extended schneid at one point eliciting boos from a frustrated Wrigley crowd. But since July 12, Bregman leads all qualified National League hitters in OPS. His experience, comportment and leadership, by all accounts, have also had a meaningful impact on Crow-Armstrong.
But pitching woes, in both the rotation and the bullpen, kept Chicago from ever seriously threatening the Brewers for the NL Central title. The Cubs started the year on something of a roller coaster, with two 10-game winning streaks and a 10-game losing streak before the calendar flipped to June. They'll enter October on something of an ice floe, with 15 runs scored in their final six contests.
Padres: San Diego has the best record in baseball since July 24. The day before, the Pads lost a rubber match in Atlanta to fall to three games under. 500. That pushed the club four games adrift of a wild-card spot, with the Cardinals, Pirates, Marlins, Nationals and Diamondbacks standing between them and a trip to October. That was the low-water mark for this team.
Since that date, the Padres have gone 41-18. They won five straight in late July, six straight in August and eight straight in September. They've lost thrice since Labor Day. The reason for the resurgence? Check out these numbers.
| Padres offensive ranks before and after July 24 | | |
| | Before | After |
| Runs/game | 4.14 (25th) | 4.95 (3rd) |
| AVG | .230 (28th) | .268 (2nd) |
| OBP | .307 (27th) | .339 (2nd) |
| SLG | .383 (27th) | .425 (2nd) |
| OPS | .689 (26th) | .764 (2nd) |
San Diego's offense went from bottom-five to top-five. Some of that is batted-ball luck and sequencing. A lot of it is Fernando Tatis Jr. turning back into a monster. Jackson Merrill had a similar rebirth. Ty France continued his bounce-back campaign. Xander Bogaerts shifted from unwatchable to capable. Unsung heroes such as Dustin Harris and Luis Rengifo got hot. The starting pitching did just enough. The game's best bullpen never stopped dominating. It's that unit, led by a cadre of flamethrowers in Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, that makes these Padres a particularly formidable October opponent.
X-factors
Cubs: Alex Bregman — specifically, his face
One week ago, Bregman was the victim of some very painful misfortune. A check-swing foul ball off the bat of Cubs first baseman Michael Busch struck Bregman in the face while he was standing in the on-deck circle. Blood dripped from below his left eye as he scurried down the dugout steps into the clubhouse. A trip to the hospital revealed multiple facial fractures. The incident kept Bregman out of the lineup until Friday, when he went 0-for-4 with a strikeout as Chicago's DH. He went 4-for-4 with two home runs and a walk in Sunday's season finale.
There's no doubt that Bregman, the textbook definition of a "grinder," will take the field in October. But at what level? He has been so integral to Chicago's lineup for the past few months that even a slightly reduced version of Bregman could unsettle things. Among active players, only his former Astros teammate Jose Altuve has taken more postseason plate appearances.
Padres: Fernando Tatis Jr.
Nothing is more meaningfully different about this year's Padres team compared to the one that went three and see-ya at Wrigley in 2025 than Fernando Tatis Jr.'s stunning offensive reemergence. Things didn't start so swimmingly this year for the swaggering outfielder, who needed 55 games to clock his first longball of this season. But since May 30, Tatis' .914 OPS ranks fourth in the NL, and his 4.9 fWAR ranks second in MLB behind only Crow-Armstrong.
This version of Tatis looks a lot like the one who took the baseball world by storm en route to finishing third in NL MVP in 2021. Will that brilliance show up in a small October sample? It usually has throughout the 27-year-old's career; he holds a 1.114 postseason OPS in 70 plate appearances. Tatis, though, has never advanced past the NLDS. Remember, he was in PED timeout when the Padres stampeded to the NLCS in 2022. Could this month be his path back to full-blown superstardom?
How they win
Cubs: The margins were razor thin when these teams lined up in the wild-card round last year, with a highlight reel of web gems from shortstop Dansby Swanson making the difference. Those games, oddly enough, were incredibly low-scoring, with Chicago snagging two 3-1 wins and San Diego edging out a 3-0 win. It's hard to imagine the Cubs and their underwhelming relief group winning that way again, particularly on the road. To advance, they'll need buckets of runs. With PCA, Bregman, Seiya Suzuki and Co., that's a real possibility.
Padres: The Padres' formula for success has been the same for the past few seasons: Shorten the game. San Diego realistically needs five innings from its starters. Then manager Craig Stammen gets to turn things over to the best relief core in baseball, led by southpaw Adrían Morejon and flamethrower Mason Miller. The Friars' starting pitching has gotten stronger as they've gotten healthy, so if Michael King in Game 1 and likely Nick Pivetta in Game 2 can each give San Diego 15 outs, the Padres have a good chance of making quick work of Chicago.

Sep 27, 2026, 9:08 PM ET
Pittsburgh Pirates outfielder Oneil Cruz (knee) did not play in his team's 4-2 win over the Detroit Tigers on Sunday due to a left knee contusion. However, Kevin Gorman of The Pittsburgh Tribune-Review reports that tests on Cruz's knee came back negative. The 27-year-old finishes 2026 hitting .280/.368/.486 with 20 home runs, 67 RBI, 65 runs scored, and 30 stolen bases across 419 plate appearances. Cruz missed over two months with a fractured hand, which may have cost him a chance at a truly elite fantasy season. The lefty slugger's .280 batting average is also likely a bit fluky, as he struck out in 33.2% of his plate appearances and batted .397 on balls in play. Still, Cruz carries elite power/speed upside for fantasy managers and profiles as one of the better outfield options for fantasy managers ahead of 2027.--Will Brady
Source: The Pittsburgh Tribune-Review - Kevin Gorman

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Alex Bregman went 4 for 4 with two home runs and four RBIs in his second game back from a frightening injury, and the Chicago Cubs beat the Boston Red Sox 6-2 on Sunday in a regular-season finale that was relocated to Tropicana Field.
Chicago is the No. 5 seed in the National League playoffs and will play a best-of-three Wild Card Series at fourth-seeded San Diego beginning Tuesday night.
Boston is the No. 5 seed in the American League playoffs and will travel to New York to open its Wild Card Series the same night against the rival Yankees.
Major League Baseball moved the Cubs-Red Sox season finale to Florida because of a weekend nor’easter that was expected to batter the Boston area into Monday. Ahead of the storm, the Red Sox swept a doubleheader from the Cubs on Friday at Fenway Park.
Bregman went 0 for 4 with a strikeout at designated hitter in the opener — five days after sustaining facial fractures when he was struck in the face by a foul ball while standing in the on-deck circle.
The three-time All-Star third baseman, who played for Boston last year, was the DH again Sunday and fared much better at the plate in his final postseason tuneup. In addition to finishing a triple shy of the cycle, he drew a walk and scored three times.
With the NL MVP award virtually locked up, Pete Crow-Armstrong singled to open the game before Cubs manager Craig Counsell immediately removed him for pinch-runner Tyrone Taylor. Bregman launched the next pitch from Tanner Houck (0-1) into the left-field seats.
Adley Rutschman hit a solo homer off Chicago starter Shota Imanaga, who was lifted after one inning with postseason seeding already decided.
Braxton Garrett (1-1) pitched five strong innings in relief for his first win since May 29, 2024. Colin Rea earned his second save.
Played at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays, the game drew 20,411 fans who had less than 48 hours’ notice to purchase tickets.
Chicago finished 89-73, three games shy of its 92-70 mark in 2025.
Boston, which was 89-73 in 2025, ended the season 87-75. The Red Sox fired manager Alex Cora following a 10-17 start and replaced him with Chad Tracy.
Under Tracy, Boston became the first team to qualify for the postseason after dropping as many as 44 of its initial 75 games.

item.content:encoded:
Last Sunday, Alex Bregman was hit in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch in Cincinnati. He suffered facial fractures and missed three games.
Bregman came back Friday as the DH and Sunday, just a bit over exactly one week since that accident, he hit two home runs and also singled, doubled and walked. His 4-for-4 afternoon led the Cubs to a 4-2 Game 162 win over the Red Sox, a game played at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
Bregman didn’t waste any time Sunday, either. Pete Crow-Armstrong led off the game with a single and then departed for pinch-runner Tyrone Taylor.
That was great to see. Bregman seemed totally locked in from the moment he stepped into the batter’s box. And that ball was crushed! [VIDEO].
Shōta Imanaga started for the Cubs and threw just the first inning, allowing a home run to Adley Rutschman. That was the 35th homer off Imanaga this year, second-most in MLB this year to Aaron Nola’s 37. Imanaga threw only 12 pitches in this game, which theoretically leaves him available to pitch in the Wild Card Series, maybe Thursday or perhaps even Wednesday. Apart from the homer, Imanaga struck out the other three hitters he faced.
Braxton Garrett, who the Cubs acquired from the Marlins at the trade deadline for minor leaguers Jonathon Long and Jace Beck and who’d been at Triple-A Iowa since, was recalled for this game and went into the game as the “bulk guy” and threw very well. Garrett threw five innings and allowed four hits and a run, though he did issue three walks. He threw 70 pitches and will be in the mix for a starting rotation spot next year.
Bregman drove in all four Cubs runs in this game and finishes with 93 RBI on the season. It’s so good to see him productive after that freak injury. Even if he is limited to DH duty for the Wild Card Series, as noted on the Marquee broadcast, he’s been the Cubs’ second-best hitter (behind PCA) all year and they are going to need that hitting. I noticed that Bregman was wearing a double-flap helmet on the basepaths, though as you can see, not when he hit the home runs.
BCB’s JohnW53 has this fact about Bregman’s two-homer afternoon:
Today’s game was Alex Bregman’s fifth of the season with multiple home runs. Pete Crow-Armstrong has seven such games; Dansby Swanson, three; and Michael Conforto, one, for a total of 16.
The Cubs had a team-record 20 such games last year. They had 19 in 2019, 18 in 1998 and 2004, and 17 in 1930 and 1958. They also had 16 in 2021.
Going into today, the Astros had 16 this year, second to the Rockies’ 18. The Padres had 15.
The Cubs flashed some glove while Garrett was in the game. Here’s a nice stop by Matt Shaw in the fifth [VIDEO].
Jacob Webb succeeded Garrett in the seventh inning and retired all three hitters he faced on just 10 pitches. I don’t think I have to tell you how important it would be if Webb could recover the form that got him 24 straight scoreless appearances before the big meltdown he had at the end of August in Seattle and Arizona.
Colin Rea entered to throw the eighth inning and also retired the Red Sox in order, on just six pitches.
The Cubs then put the game away with a three-run ninth. Miguel Amaya led off with a single and went to third on a single by Taylor. That brought up Bregman, and he came through yet again with this RBI double [VIDEO].
Fact about Bregman’s game from John:
Bregman is just the sixth Cub to hit multiple homers and also have at least one double, one single and one walk. He is the first to do so on the road.
Pete Crow-Armstrong did it in on Aug. 17 in the Cubs’ 10-inning, 7-5 win at home over the White Sox, with his second homer walking it off.
The four others:
Hank Sauer: May 2, 1954, in an 18-10, eight-inning loss to the Pirates
Ryne Sandberg: Aug. 10, 1989, in a 16-13 loss to the Phillies
Corey Patterson: Sept. 7, 2004, in a 7-6, 12-inning loss to the Expos
Chris Coghlan: Sept. 20, 2014, in an 8-7 win over the Dodgers
All had two homers, one double, one single and one walk.
Taylor stopped at third on Bregman’s double, but he then scored on this sac fly by Gabriel Arias [VIDEO].
As mentioned on the Marquee broadcast, Arias is a very good bench player. He can play all infield positions and his bat plays well enough, a really useful guy to have around. That made it 5-2. Ian Happ then struck out, but Michael Conforto doubled, scoring Bregman to give the Cubs a four-run lead [VIDEO].
Rea remained in the game in the ninth to finish up, and he recorded his second save. Here’s the final out [VIDEO].
In other postseason-related news, the Phillies won Sunday and so they take the final wild card spot and will face the Braves in Atlanta in another Wild Card Series beginning Tuesday. The Rangers lost to the Twins, which clinched the A.L. West title for the Astros (who are leading the A’s late and likely will finish 81-81). Houston will host the White Sox in a Wild Card Series starting Tuesday.
One more game note from John:
The Cubs’ six runs made their final total 850, their fourth most in the Modern Era, which began in 1901. They scored 998 in 1930, 982 in 1929 and 855 in 2008. They played 156 games in the first two seasons and 161 in the last.
And for whatever it’s worth, the win gave the Cubs an 89-73 record to the Red Sox’ 87-75. That means that if, somehow, those two clubs meet in the World Series, the Cubs would have home field. The Cubs have the better record over four of the six American League postseason teams; only the Rays and Yankees are better.
So the Cubs will now head to San Diego to begin their own Wild Card Series against the Padres Tuesday evening. I’ll have lots to say about that over the next couple of days here, of course. Michael King has been announced as the Padres starter, but no Cubs starter has yet been named. It could be Matthew Boyd, who’d be going on normal rest, as he last pitched on Thursday against the Marlins at Wrigley Field.
Game time Tuesday is late, so get rested up! 9 p.m. CT, with the game on NBC Sports Network (cable) and streaming on Peacock.
Go Cubs!

Shota Imanaga doesn’t need anyone else’s help celebrating.
The Cubs pitcher went viral after repeatedly blasting himself in the face with beer during the team’s wild clubhouse celebration after clinching a spot in the postseason Thursday.
Naturally, Imanaga had an explanation for the madness.
“This is Japanese style,” Imanaga said while holding a bottle in each hand. “Japanese misogi.”
Imanaga then turned both bottles toward himself and sprayed the beer directly onto his head and face, bobbing up and down into the streams as his teammates laughed around him.
“Self-service!” Imanaga said.
The Cubs leaned into the moment themselves, posting the video on social media captioned: “Who needs bottle service when you have self-service?”
During an interview with Marquee Sports Network’s Taylor McGregor amid the clubhouse celebration, Imanaga was showered with champagne by his teammates.
His response?
“Yummy!”
Chicago officially punched its postseason ticket with a 2-1 victory over the Marlins at Wrigley Field, securing a playoff berth for the second consecutive season.
Seiya Suzuki tied the game with his 26th home run of the season in the fifth inning before Nico Hoerner drove home Ian Happ for the eventual winning run in the sixth.
Pete Crow-Armstrong also stole his 40th base of the season in the victory, giving him 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases and making him just the seventh player in MLB history to accomplish the feat.
Imanaga has played his part in getting Chicago back to the playoffs for the second consecutive season.
The 33-year-old left-hander went 11-10 with a 3.74 ERA while remaining a fixture in Chicago’s starting rotation throughout the season.
He also recorded 171 strikeouts in 173 ⅓ innings pitched in 2026.
Last year, the Cubs went 92-70 and took care of the Padres in the wild-card round before falling to the Brewers in five games in the NLDS.
Imanaga, who was an All-Star two seasons ago, turned 33 earlier this month and has a career 3.44 ERA and a 35-21 record.

レッドソックスは本拠地フェンウェイパークで行われたカブスとのダブルヘッダー第1試合に4-3で逆転勝利。ア・リーグの第5シードに入ることが確定し、ワイルドカードシリーズでは同地区の宿敵ヤンキースと対戦することになった。カブスの鈴木誠也は「2番・右翼」でスタメン出場し、初回の第1打席で四球を選んで先制のホームイン。しかし、その後はピッチャーゴロ、空振り三振、ショートゴロ、空振り三振と快音響かず、4打数無安打1四球で今季の打撃成績は打率.268、OPS.837となった。 レッドソックス先発のアレック・ガンボアは初回、1死から鈴木に四球を与え、2死後にタイロン・テイラーにレフトへのタイムリー二塁打を浴びて先制点を献上。二回は1死一、二塁の場面でミゲル・アマヤに2点タイムリー二塁打を浴び、2回4安打3失点で降板した。 しかし、ガンボア降板後、レッドソックス投手陣がカブス打線を封じた。2番手のジェイク・ベネットは3回2/3を3安打無失点に抑え、六回2死一塁の場面で登板した3番手のグレッグ・ワイサートも1回1/3を無失点。八回と九回は4番手のレイモンド・バーゴスが打者6人をパーフェクトに抑える好投を見せた。 レッドソックス打線は二回までカブス先発のクレイ・ホームズに無得点に抑えられていたが、三回にエラー絡みで1点を返すと、五回には1死二、三塁のチャンスを作り、ホームズを降板に追い込んだ。このあと、2番手のケイレブ・シールバーからアドリー・ラッチマンが2点タイムリーを放ち、3-3の同点に。リリーフ陣の奮闘に打線が応え、試合を振り出しに戻した。 2死満塁のピンチを切り抜けた直後の七回には勝ち越しのチャンスが到来。ロマン・アンソニーがライトへの三塁打を放ち、1死三塁となった。ここでコナー・ウォンがタイムリー二塁打を放ち、4-3と勝ち越しに成功。この1点を守り切って今季86勝目を挙げ、ア・リーグの第5シードを確定させた。 なお、カブスとレッドソックスは3連戦の最終戦を今日にスライドしてダブルヘッダーを開催し、明日がシーズン最終戦となる予定だったが、ボストンの天気が悪いため、明日の試合をレギュラーシーズン最終日となる27日（同28日）にスライドして開催地をレイズの本拠地であるトロピカーナフィールドに変更。確実に試合を消化できる日程が組まれることになった。

item.content:encoded:
Sep 23, 2026, 11:45 AM ET
Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (back) remains out of action for Game 1 of Wednesday's doubleheader at Camden Yards against the division-rival Baltimore Orioles, per MLB.com. Sean Keys will make another start at first base and will bat fifth against Orioles right-hander Chris Bassitt. Guerrero is considered day-to-day right now in the final week of the regular season after departing Sunday's game early against the Texas Rangers due to tightness in his lower back. It is something that the 27-year-old Canadian slugger has already dealt with this year, and it could explain why the six-time All-Star has had a very disappointing 2026 campaign. Guerrero enters play on Wednesday with a .263/.336/.359 slash line, a .695 OPS, only nine home runs, 56 RBI, 71 runs scored, and seven steals across his 529 at-bats. Toronto entered play on Wednesday four games out of the final wild-card spot in the American League and on the brink of elimination. If they lose the first game of Wednesday's doubleheader, Guerrero could be shut down for the rest of the week.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com

Jeremy Pena Suffers Wrist Injury on Tuesday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 23, 2026, 11:38 AM ET
Houston Astros shortstop Jeremy Pena (wrist) was hit on the right wrist with a 96.4 mph sinker in Tuesday's game against the Seattle Mariners and was removed in the eighth inning, according to Chandler Rome of The Athletic. Pena attempted to stay in the contest, but he was eventually replaced by Nick Allen at shortstop after going 1-for-4 at the plate with two runs scored and two strikeouts. The Astros likely sent Pena for X-rays, and we will pass along the results when we have them. Fantasy managers will want to check back later to see if the Astros' starting shortstop will be available for Wednesday's game in Seattle against the Mariners. Losing Pena for the rest of the final week of the 2026 regular season would be a huge blow, with the Astros going into Wednesday's action tied for first in the American League West with the Texas Rangers. The 29-year-old Pena has missed time this year due to various injuries, but he has been solid when healthy, slashing .275/.325/.469 with a .795 OPS, 20 home runs, 51 RBI, 77 runs scored, and 10 stolen bases in 107 games across 461 plate appearances.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Chandler Rome
Ceddanne Rafaela Set to Return From Injured List on Wednesday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 11:08 PM ET
The Boston Red Sox plan to activate second baseman/outfielder Ceddanne Rafaela (quadriceps) from the 10-day injured list on Wednesday, manager Chad Tracy told Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Rafaela should be back in the starting lineup for Boston in Game 2 of the series against the Cleveland Guardians. He has been out since Sept. 6 with a strained right quad but did not play in a minor-league rehab game. The 26-year-old continues to contribute across most fantasy baseball categories, but he could be a little rusty upon his return to the big leagues as the Red Sox try to get him going again before the wild-card series against the division-rival New York Yankees begins next week. Rafaela made the All-Star team for the first time in his career in 2026 and will return to a nice .282/.317/.443 slash line, a career-high .760 OPS, 16 home runs, 70 RBI, 17 stolen bases, and 67 runs scored across 135 games played. If Rafaela hits a home run by the end of the weekend, he will have a new career high in home runs in his fourth year in the majors.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Sep 22, 2026, 11:00 PM ET
Chicago Cubs manager Craig Counsell said that third baseman Alex Bregman (face) will not be placed on the injured list and could return to the team's lineup before the end of the regular season, per Russell Dorsey of Yahoo Sports. Bregman was struck in the face by a foul ball while standing in the on-deck circle during Chicago's game against the Cincinnati Reds on Sunday. The 32-year-old suffered multiple facial fractures, but he was able to avoid surgery and appears to be on track to return to the Cubs for the postseason. Across 693 plate appearances in 2026, Bregman is hitting .262/.352/.452 with 26 home runs, 89 RBI, 89 runs scored, and three stolen bases. He's been one of the best hitters in baseball in the second half of the season, hitting .296 with 17 home runs across 262 plate appearances since the All-Star break. With Bregman in the middle of it, the Cubs lineup profiles as arguably the best in MLB in 2026.--Will Brady
Source: Yahoo Sports - Russell Dorsey
Sep 22, 2026, 10:52 PM ET
Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said that closer Aroldis Chapman (lat) "should be cleared in the next day or two," per Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. Chapman has not pitched since September 13 due to lat tightness, but it appears as though the 38-year-old is on the doorstep of a return to his role in the ninth inning for the Red Sox. Across 50 2/3 innings (52 games) in 2026, Chapman has recorded a 1.95 ERA and 1.14 WHIP with 68 strikeouts and 34 saves. The veteran left-hander has not been quite as dominant as he was in his first season with Boston in 2025, but he's still posted an excellent 32.4% strikeout rate and blown just two save chances. When healthy, Chapman remains a must-start closer for fantasy managers.--Will Brady
Source: The Boston Globe - Tim Healey
Joc Pederson Placed on 10-Day Injured List


Will Brady




Sep 22, 2026, 10:47 PM ET
Texas Rangers designated hitter Joc Pederson (hand) has been placed on the 10-day injured list (retroactive to September 19) due to a fracture in his left hand. The 34-year-old had been attempting to play through the injury, but it appears that he and the team ultimately came to the conclusion that a trip to the IL was necessary. Pederson bounced back from a brutal 2025 campaign with a solid year at the plate in 2026, hitting .235/.329/.487 with 26 home runs, 53 RBI, 56 runs scored, and two stolen bases. The veteran lefty slugger re-established himself as an excellent source of big-side platoon power, posting an 11.2% barrel rate and a 50.7% hard-hit rate. With Pederson now sidelined through at least the remainder of the regular season, Texas has rotated shortstop Corey Seager and backup catcher Elias Diaz through its DH spot.--Will Brady
Source: Texas Rangers
Landen Roupp Shut Down for Remainder of 2026


Will Brady




Sep 22, 2026, 10:34 PM ET
San Francisco Giants starting pitcher Landen Roupp told reporters on Tuesday that his 2026 season is over, per Justice delos Santos of The Mercury News. Per delos Santos, Roupp feels fine physically, but is being shut down because he has already blown past his previous career high in innings pitched. Across 155 innings (29 starts) this year, the 28-year-old recorded a 9-14 record with a 4.01 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, and 143 strikeouts. Roupp limits power (0.64 HR/9), which has helped him develop into a capable innings eater for fantasy managers. However, the right-hander's production upside is limited by his middling strikeout rate (21.8%) and his poor walk rate (11.4%). Between his penchant for allowing walks and generating ground balls, Roupp is unlikely to be an asset in the WHIP category without a change in his approach on the mound.--Will Brady
Source: The Mercury News - Justice delos Santos
Sep 22, 2026, 10:29 PM ET
Seattle Mariners closer Andres Munoz (knee) "should be ok" and could be available to his team on Tuesday night after undergoing an MRI on his injured knee, per Shannon Drayer of Seattle Sports 710. Munoz was pulled from his most recent appearance on Sunday after tweaking his right knee, but he appears to have avoided serious injury. It's been a disappointing year overall for the 27-year-old, who has recorded a 4.24 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 89 strikeouts, and 28 saves across 57 1/3 innings (61 games). Munoz has struggled with home runs (1.41 HR/9) and has blown a career-high 10 saves. However, the hard-throwing right-hander is still averaging 99.7 miles per hour on his fastball and has logged an elite 37.1% strikeout rate. Heading into 2027, Munoz could be an excellent buy-low candidate for fantasy managers.--Will Brady
Source: Seattle Sports 710 - Shannon Drayer
Sep 22, 2026, 10:22 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell (groin) is scheduled to start against the San Francisco Giants on Saturday, per David Vassegh of AM 570 LA Sports. Snell exited early from his most recent start on September 16 due to a groin issue. However, it appears that Snell will be able to make one final start before the postseason. It's been a lost season due to injury for the 33-year-old, who has missed time due to elbow and shoulder troubles. Still, Snell has been effective when healthy, recording a 4-1 record with a 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, and 52 strikeouts across 38 2/3 innings (eight starts). Fantasy managers may be able to get one more solid outing from Snell on Saturday, but the Dodgers also have little incentive to push his pitch count deep into the game.--Will Brady
Source: AM 570 LA Sports - David Vassegh
Sep 22, 2026, 10:11 PM ET
Atlanta Braves outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. (shin) exited early from his team's 4-0 loss to the Cincinnati Reds on Tuesday after fouling a ball off his leg. Per Mark Bowman of MLB.com, X-rays on the leg were negative, and the star outfielder is now being listed as day-to-day with a shin contusion. Acuna Jr. was hitless in one plate appearance before leaving the game. While it appears that he's avoided a serious injury, Atlanta could still choose to be extremely cautious with Acuna Jr. in the final week of the regular season. The Braves have already clinched the National League East title and are likely locked into the number three seed in the NL. Across 455 plate appearances in 2026, Acuna Jr. is hitting .259/.352/.462 with 20 home runs, 55 RBI, 60 runs scored, and eight stolen bases. If he misses any time, Braves outfielders Brewer Hicklen and Mike Yastrzemski would likely see an increase in at-bats.--Will Brady
Source: MLB.com - Mark Bowman
Shohei Ohtani Expected to Return on Wednesday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 7:50 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani (knee) is expected to be activated from the injured list on Wednesday, as had been the hope, manager Dave Roberts told Sonja Chen of MLB.com. Ohtani is getting ready to return from a stay on the IL that lasted for several weeks. The four-time MVP has not made a start as a pitcher since July 3 against the Padres, and he is not expected to be an option on the mound for the Dodgers at all the rest of the regular season or postseason. But Roberts expects Ohtani to be ready to return on Wednesday against San Diego as the team's primary designated hitter. They will want the 32-year-old Japanese superstar to get some live at-bats going into the final weekend of the regular season before the playoffs begin in October. Ohtani's two-way status has taken a toll on him physically in 2026, although he still has hit a strong .277/.380/.522 with 30 home runs, 80 RBI, 11 stolen bases, and 89 runs scored in 130 games. While he probably will not win a fourth straight MVP award, Ohtani can definitely still help the Dodgers win an unprecedented third straight World Series title if he is past his knee and biceps injuries that have bothered him for around half the season.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Sonja Chen
Kyle Tucker Back in Action Tuesday Against Padres


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 7:44 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Kyle Tucker (knee, shin) is starting in right field and is hitting fifth for Tuesday's series opener against the division-rival San Diego Padres and right-hander Michael King, per MLB.com. Tucker was held out of the series finale on Sunday against the division-rival San Francisco Giants with a minor knee/shin injury, but he is ready for this week in a crucial series at Dodger Stadium. The 29-year-old lefty slugger has not had the first season in L.A. that he envisioned, and he enters Tuesday's action with a .234/.334/.393 slash line, a .727 OPS, 17 home runs, 70 RBI, 88 runs scored, and 11 stolen bases across 148 games and 602 plate appearances. The former first-rounder's production has picked up in September, though, which has been good timing for the Dodgers with two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani (knee, biceps) on the injured list. Tucker has hit .283 (17-for-60) with a 1.059 OPS, six homers, and 13 RBI in 19 games in September. Against King in 12 career at-bats, he is hitting .083 with one RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Xavier Edwards Still Sidelined Against Cubs


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 5:32 PM ET
Miami Marlins middle infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) remains out of action for Tuesday's series opener at Wrigley Field against the Chicago Cubs, according to MLB.com. Jared Serna will make the start at the keystone for the Fish on Tuesday and will bat ninth against Cubs left-hander Shota Imanaga. Edwards is missing a second straight start after he injured his thumb on Saturday in San Diego against the Padres. The Marlins are eliminated from postseason contention, but the hope is that Edwards will be able to return during the final week of the 2026 regular season. In his fourth season in the big leagues with the Marlins, the 27-year-old has had another strong season, hitting .280/.360/.371 with a .730 OPS, a career-high six home runs, 52 RBI, 21 stolen bases, and 61 runs scored in 142 games played and 595 plate appearances. Edwards is more of a contact-oriented slap hitter, but he now has three straight seasons with 20-plus stolen bases while being eligible in Yahoo leagues at both second base and shortstop.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sep 22, 2026, 4:58 PM ET
In a surprise move, the New York Mets announced on Tuesday that they agreed to a three-year contract with Andy Green to make him their full-time manager. The Mets have elected to remove Green's interim tag, and he will now be with the team through the 2029 season. Since taking over for previous manager Carlos Mendoza at the end of June, the Mets have gone 37-38. "Andy has connected with and pushed our players to perform, despite the disappointment of the season," owners Steve and Alex Cohen said in a statement. "Over the last several months, he has brought discipline, accountability and positivity to the clubhouse, attributes we were seeking in our next manager." Green was previously the Mets' vice president of player development before becoming the interim manager in New York. He managed the San Diego Padres for almost four seasons from 2016 to 2019 and went 274-366.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Mets
Cade Cavalli Done for the Year


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 4:52 PM ET
Washington Nationals right-hander Cade Cavalli is done for the year and will not make another start in the final week of the 2026 season, according to Spencer Nusbaum of The Athletic. Cavalli is healthy, but the Nationals will shut him down given all of his innings and where they are in the standings with no hope of a playoff berth. The 28-year-old former first-rounder in 2020 from the University of Oklahoma had a breakout 2026 campaign in his first full year in the big leagues in D.C., going 13-5 with a 3.02 ERA (3.25 FIP) and 1.15 WHIP with a career-high 200 strikeouts and 48 walks in 169 2/3 innings pitched across his 32 starts. Going into the year, Cavalli had only made 11 starts and had missed all of 2023 after having Tommy John surgery. Washington recently rewarded the rising young arm with a four-year, $47 million contract extension last week. Cavalli will be an intriguing starting-pitching target in all fantasy formats next year after raising his strikeout rate to a career-high 28.3% in 2026.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Athletic - Spencer Nusbaum
Brandon Nimmo Returns From Illness on Tuesday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 4:44 PM ET
Texas Rangers outfielder Brandon Nimmo (illness) is starting in right field and batting fifth on Tuesday against the visiting New York Mets and left-hander Sean Manaea, according to MLB.com. Nimmo is feeling good enough to play on Tuesday against his old team after a scheduled day off on Monday. The 33-year-old has not lived up to expectations in his first season with the Rangers in 2026, slashing .260/.325/.407 with a .732 OPS, 14 home runs, 61 RBI, 61 runs scored, and seven stolen bases across his 570 at-bats after reaching the 20-homer mark in his final three seasons with the Mets, including a career-high 25 round-trippers in 2025. The former first-rounder in 2011 has slumped in the final month of the regular season, too, going 15-for-66 (.227) with zero home runs, four doubles, eight RBI, five runs scored, six walks, and 22 strikeouts in 17 games in September. Nimmo will attempt to turn things around in the final week of the season and try to help Texas win the American League West division. He has actually hit much better against lefties this year, going 59-for-179 (.330) against them with five of his 14 homers on the year.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Jack Flaherty Expected to Pitch This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 22, 2026, 4:35 PM ET
Detroit Tigers right-hander Jack Flaherty (forearm) is expected to come off the 15-day injured list to make one more appearance this weekend against the Pittsburgh Pirates in the final series of the season, according to Cody Stavenhagen of The Athletic. Flaherty has been sidelined since late July with inflammation in his right flexor, and without going on a minor-league rehab assignment, it seems likely that the veteran hurler will be a piggyback option for the Tigers this weekend in a meaningless game for either veteran Justin Verlander or pitching prospect River Ryan. The 30-year-old has gone 3-8 with a 4.59 ERA (4.09 FIP) and 1.41 WHIP with 102 strikeouts and 42 walks in 86 1/3 innings pitched across his 19 starts in 2026 in his second year in Motown. item.content:encoded:
It’s time for both sides of this great baseball town to come together.
No, not the fans. We know better than to ask for that.
Rather, we mean the Cubs and White Sox themselves, for — a doff of the cap and a drumroll, please — the Sun-Times’ 2026 All-City Team is here.
Beat writers Vinnie Duber (Cubs) and James Fegan (Sox) joined frequent baseball scribe Jeff Agrest and yours truly in selecting a 17-man team: one player at each position in the field, a designated hitter, four starting pitchers, three relievers — one of them designated as closer — and a manager.
Four ironclad rules guided our process:
1. This is a 2026 honor. Reputation doesn’t matter.
2. If it’s too close to call at certain positions, lean into which players we’d rather write into a playoff lineup.
3. All players must appear at their primary positions. No exceptions!
4. OK, fine, Alex Bregman and Miguel Vargas both need to be in there somehow. Besides, if we journalists followed the rules, how would everybody know to hate us?
Our team:
SP1: Sean Burke, Sox
Leads Chicago starters in ERA, strikeouts, opponent batting average — closest we’ve got to an ace.
SP2: Shota Imanaga, Cubs
Other than the gopher balls — so many gopher balls — lefty has been effective.
SP3: Davis Martin, Sox
Sox were 10-1 over his first 11 starts. Finishing kick has been strong, too. (As for in between, don’t ask.)
SP4: Matthew Boyd, Cubs
Still one guy who — if locked in — can get you to the seventh inning of a playoff game.
C: Carson Kelly, Cubs
Good hitter, even better with men in scoring position. Not an All-Star, but we’ll take him.
1B: Munetaka Murakami, Sox
Hamstring injury derailed spectacular start. Still, top 10 in AL in homers, walks is big-time.
2B: Chase Meidroth, Sox
Sorry, Nico Hoerner, but this was an easy call. Meidroth has simply been the better batsman.
3B: Alex Bregman, Cubs
One of the best second halves in baseball, combined with stellar glove work. Tough call, though.
SS: Dansby Swanson, Cubs
Just too great on “D” — and Colson Montgomery didn’t get on base enough to unseat him.
LF: Tristan Peters, Sox
South Side’s best outfielder — an All-Star, don’t forget — gets bumped over by you-know-who.
CF: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
But you knew this already. Not bad, Mr. MVP.
RF: Seiya Suzuki, Cubs
His RISP work wasn’t the best, but you take the offensive totals every time.
DH: Miguel Vargas, Sox
Sox’ MVP — there’s no debate about that — simply has to be in our lineup.
RP: Bryan Hudson, Sox
Quality lefty with multiple impressive scoreless streaks and pinpoint control all second half.
RP: Sean Newcomb, Sox
Lefty hangs on to a spot despite a rough September.
Closer: Grant Taylor, Sox
The best reliever in town and the only sane choice for this role.
Manager: Craig Counsell, Cubs
Potentially winning 90 despite one pitching problem after another is nothing to sneeze at.
DISSENSIONS IN THE RANKS
In the end, we were in unison on all but three positions. Fegan backed Vargas at third base and Will Venable at manager, and I wanted Sam Antonacci in left.
Fegan on Vargas: Bregman and Vargas are statistically even, so let’s get sentimental. Vargas has been the rock of a Sox offense otherwise defined by streaks. He’s the proof of concept of their newfound ability to improve hitters. A universally beloved bilingual glue guy in a loose clubhouse, Vargas is the team MVP who laughs hard and works harder. Without him, Sox leadership is talking “meaningful progress” rather than playoffs.
Greenberg on Antonacci: His defense is more mosh pit than ballet, but throw him off his spot because of it? Come on, man. He’s always on base, hits in the clutch and plays with his rear end on fire. How do you not love a young cat with a perverse desire to stand in front of 96 mph and get drilled by it? These Sox aren’t these Sox without his signature brand of — how to put it? — Antonacciness.
Fegan on Venable: His in-game moves miss the mark at times; inarguable since he readily fesses up without prompting. But with how naturally fans and commentators have shifted to second-guessing every crucial move in a division chase, it might surprise locally how well Venable does in AL manager of the year voting, or how the baseball world still views his team cracking the playoffs as coaching alchemy, or how much his constant tinkering is not unique but actually–gasp!–the Sox adhering to modern trends.
Contributing: James Fegan, Vinnie Duber, Jeff Agrest

item.content:encoded:
The Cubs are as close to securing a trip back to the postseason as possible.
The North Siders need just a single win, or a single D-backs loss, over the regular season’s final week to clinch a spot in the NL Wild Card round.
Who will the Cubs play? And where will those games be played? Those questions won’t be answered until next weekend, most likely.
But with just six games remaining until playoff baseball, who will the Cubs need to step up in order to make a run at the World Series in a National League field filled with strong contenders such as the Brewers, Dodgers and Braves?
Here’s a look at who the Cubs need to do their part to get back to the Fall Classic for the first time since 2016:
Who will step up at the back end of the 'pen?
Who will close games? This is by far the Cubs’ biggest, and potentially most important, question that needs to be answered. Will it be Jacob Webb, who leads the team with nine saves, or will former closer Daniel Palencia, who just spun two scoreless innings in one of his most impressive outings of the year, be able to take that role? Manager Craig Counsell, who has used 14 pitchers to record saves this season, will be tasked with piecing together a bullpen that has limited experience in those situations.
The Cubs need Webb, who spun a scoreless outing in 24 straight appearances from June to August, to get back into form after allowing 11 runs over his past 7 2/3 innings (nine games). If Palencia, who has thrown 6 1/3 straight scoreless innings, can also replicate his success from 2025, it could be a major boost for a club that entered Cincinnati converting just four of its past 12 save opportunities.
Deadline acquisition Ryan Zeferjahn and lefty Ryan Rolison could also play a big factor late in games, but there’s also a secret weapon waiting out in the bullpen …
Can Cabrera be a reliable relief option?
That brings us to Edward Cabrera, who returned from a recurring blister injury on his pitching hand on Sept. 15 in a multi-inning relief role. That will be his job going forward as the Cubs hope shorter outings can not only keep him healthy, but potentially provide a small uptick in velocity. Cabrera’s first relief experience had mixed results (two runs in 2 1/3 IP), but he came out of the bullpen Sunday and tossed a scoreless inning on just nine pitches.
The best-case scenario of this temporary move to the bullpen? Cabrera turns into this year’s version of the Dodgers’ Roki Sasaki, which would immediately help stabilize the back end of the Cubs’ bullpen. Cabrera’s season hasn’t gone to plan, posting a 5.68 ERA in 15 starts between three stints on the injured list, but he still has a chance to make a significant impact when it matters most.
PCA still doing MVP things in October
Is it really fair to ask more of Pete Crow-Armstrong? After going yard again Sunday, the Cubs slugger is tied with Philadelphia’s Kyle Schwarber for the most home runs in the Major Leagues. He leads Chicago in batting average (.280), homers (45), RBIs (107), stolen bases (38), runs scored (118), on-base percentage (.371), hits (170), triple (eight) and games played (156). Got all that? Simply put, he’s put together one of the most impressive offensive seasons in Cubs history and he’s not done.
But he will need others to contribute in October. While run production starts with Crow-Armstrong, even if he performs to his NL MVP front-runner ability, he can’t do it all himself. The North Siders have to count on Seiya Suzuki, Dansby Swanson, Ian Happ, Alex Bregman and Michael Busch below him in the lineup to generate scoring chances.
Holmes stepping up as playoff ace
Clay Holmes and Matthew Boyd are the clear No. 1 and No. 2 options for the playoffs, but Counsell hasn’t yet revealed who will pitch in the all-important Game 1. Holmes had a strong August (1.55 ERA in five starts) in his return to the big leagues after missing nearly three months with a right fibula fracture, but he’s allowed 16 ER in just 15 1/3 IP across three starts in September (9.39 ERA).
That’s a worrying trend for a club with limited starting options in the postseason, but Shota Imanaga has stabilized recently after a down stretch in August, and veteran Kevin Gausman can provide multiple innings in whatever role the Cubs need during the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
After going 0-for-10 with four strikeouts in the first two games of this series, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had himself another big day in the third contest. PCA singled, doubled, homered and stole a base and helped lead the Cubs to a 9-1 blowout of the Reds, a victory tempered by a freak injury to Alex Bregman. More on the latter anon, first let’s wrap this win.
The Cubs got on the board in the first inning. PCA led off the game with a single and stole second, his 38th [VIDEO].
The Cubs extended their lead in the third. PCA led off with a double. A note on that double from BCB’s JohnW53:
With his third-inning double, Pete Crow-Armstrong has at least 30 homers, doubles and steals.
Only one Cub had done that before: PCA, last year.
Forty players on other teams have done it, 12 of them also multiple times. PCA is among 10 with two. Alfonso Soriano did it four times; Barry Bonds and Jose Ramirez, three.
It was noted on the Marquee broadcast that PCA’s 40-HR, 30-double, 30-steal year is the first ever by a MLB center fielder — nope, not Willie Mays, not Ken Griffey Jr., no one, until now. I’ve said it before, but don’t ever forget what you are seeing from Pete this year — it is truly historic.
Anyway, PCA then went to third on a ground out by Seiya Suzuki. The Cubs then loaded the bases on walks drawn by Michael Busch and Bregman.
Per the Marquee broadcast, that’s 22 bases-loaded walks for the Cubs this year, the most in MLB.
With the bases still loaded, Michael Conforto struck out, but Pedro Ramirez followed with a two-run single to make it 5-0 [VIDEO].
Now to the Bregman incident in the fourth inning. With two out, Busch hit a foul ball that struck Bregman, who was in the on-deck circle, in the face. Bregman immediately left the game and was replaced by Matt Shaw. Here’s what that looked like [VIDEO].
Per Craig Counsell’s postgame remarks, the ball hit Bregman in the cheekbone, which is swollen. There was also a facial cut, but we don’t know anything beyond that. Hopefully it’s not too serious and Bregman doesn’t have a concussion.
While all this was going on, David Peterson was sailing along, striking out seven over the first four innings. The Reds made it 5-1 on a solo homer by JJ Bleday in the fourth.
The Cubs got that run right back in the fifth on a solo homer by Michael Conforto, his 15th [VIDEO].
If you’re keeping track:
Kyle Tucker, 16 HR, 515 AB
Michael Conforto, 15 HR, 294 AB
That blast tied PCA with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. The Cubs also lead MLB in home runs with 217; as noted on the Marquee broadcast, the last time the Cubs led all of baseball in home runs was 1958, led by Ernie Banks with 47 in his first MVP season.
Peterson completed six innings, allowing three hits and just the one run on Bleday’s homer. Here are his seven strikeouts [VIDEO].
More on Peterson’s afternoon from BCB’s JohnW53:
David Peterson’s quality start was his fifth as a Cub, fourth most on the team. Shota Imanaga has 14, as many as the next two combined: Matthew Boyd, eight, and Colin Rea, six. Edward Cabrera and Jameson Taillon both have four. Five others have one to three.
Peterson could be a valuable weapon in the postseason, either as a starter or out of the bullpen.
The Cubs weren’t done homering, either. After Caleb Thielbar threw a scoreless seventh, Suzuki lofted his 25th into the batter’s eye to make it 9-1 [VIDEO].
